advances: Recomputing every retained prefix's own adaptive saddle does not make the largest surplus-paying prefix rule compatible with a constant original-mass loss when that rule removes both sites \(2\) and \(3\) outside the selected prefix. An exact legal family makes every nonempty prefix fail its own surplus test, while the resulting all-binary fallback loses an unbounded factor. All prefix saddles in the family have every active height above half the cap. This refutes the specified selection criterion only. It does not refute deletion of site \(3\) alone or any lower bound for the original cubic depth moment.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted 69083720ffaaff7c supplies only the stated scalar identities and bounds, the canonical auxiliary-law conventions, and the motivation for the surplus test (A). Binary scalar calculations, localization of every retained minimizer, the failure of the rule for every choice among minimizers, and the original-mass comparison are proved above.
proof:
The family (B) satisfies every required integrality and convexity condition: \(B\ge2\), \(C_{4,i}=2B_i-1\), and the interpolated slopes are \(1,B-1,B-1\). The cap is finite, the zero tilt is allowed, and all supports contain the zero atom. Tied costs may be ordered arbitrarily; every prefix has \(j\) identical four-site coordinates and \(k-j\) identical binary coordinates. We prove the assertions for every choice of global minimizer.

For one binary coordinate the only displacement at either root is zero. Its scalar functions are therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\rm bin}(s)&=1+e^{-4s},
&Z_{\rm bin,scalar}(s)&=1+e^{-s},\\
\mu_{\rm bin}(s)&=\frac{e^{-4s}}{1+e^{-4s}},
&R_{\rm bin}(s)&=s^2(1+\mu_{\rm bin}(s))\le2s^2.
\end{aligned} \tag{1}
$$
The notation \(Z_{\rm bin,scalar}\) denotes only the scalar sum; \(Z_{\rm bin}\) continues to denote the complete epigraph mass in the statement. Also
$$
\delta_{\rm bin}(s)
 =\log\cosh(2s)-4\log\cosh(s/2)\le2s^2. \tag{2}
$$
Indeed, \(\log\cosh x\le x^2/2\), obtained by integrating \(\tanh x\le x\) for \(x\ge0\). Direct differentiation gives \((\log P_{\rm bin})'/4=-\mu_{\rm bin}\).

For one four-site coordinate in (B), use the canonical \(u=s\), \(v=sB\), and put \(q=e^{-2v/3}\). Its fourth scaled cost is \(sC_{4,i}=2v-u\). Thus \(v_i=v\) for every full coordinate in the notation of accepted \(69083720ffaaff7c\). Its exact scalar kernels give
$$
\begin{aligned}
K_s(1)&=e^{-4u/3}+2q,\\
K_s(2)&=3e^{-4v/3},\\
P(s)&=1+(e^{-4u/3}+2q)^3+27e^{-4v}+e^{-4(2v-u)}.
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
$$
Here \(P=P_i\) for any full coordinate. The \(56\)-tuple expansion described with (13) of accepted \(69083720ffaaff7c\) has nonnegative energies, so \(P(s)\le56\) for \(s\ge0\). The one-coordinate estimates (13)-(14) of that accepted fact apply literally with \(g_i=(0,1,B,2B-1)\). In particular, for \(0<s\le1\), \(v\ge24\), they give
$$
\mu_{\rm four}(s)\le1+64Bq,\qquad
R_{\rm four}(s)\le2s^2+128v^2q. \tag{4}
$$
For every \(0<s\le s_{\max}\), they also give
\(R_{\rm four}(s)<256\), \(s\mu_{\rm four}(s)<32\), and
\((\log P)'/4=-\mu_{\rm four}\). These are only scalar inputs; no homogeneous-product conclusion is being used for the mixed retained laws.

First localize every minimizing rate. Put
$$
\bar s=\frac{24+3\log(2k)}B
 \le\frac{30k}B<\frac1{100}. \tag{5}
$$
Here \(\log(2k)\le2k\) and \(k\ge1\). Since \(\beta=0\), the original tail is \(f_t=2B-t+1\). If \(s\ge1/B\), no integer \(t<B\) is active for \(\mathcal F\), because its forward increment is positive:
$$
s-\log\frac{2B-t+1}{2B-t}
 \ge\frac1B-\log\frac{B+2}{B+1}>0
 \qquad(0\le t<B). \tag{6}
$$
Thus both one-sided derivatives of \(\mathcal F\) at such a rate are at least \(B\).

For \(\bar s\le s\le1\), the scalar bounds (1) and (4) imply
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mu^{[j]}(s)+L^{[j]}(s)}B
 &\le\frac{k+40\sqrt{2k}}B
       +64kq+40\sqrt{128}\sqrt{kq},\\
q&\le e^{-16}(2k)^{-2}.
\end{aligned} \tag{7}
$$
For the radius estimate, first use
\(V_s^{[j]}\le2ks^2+128jv^2q\), and then use
\(\sqrt{a+b}\le\sqrt a+\sqrt b\) and \(j\le k\).
The three terms on the right of (7) are respectively less than \(1/1024\), \(1/4096\), and \(15/16\). For the first, use
\(k+40\sqrt{2k}\le61k\) and \(B=2^{16}k^2\). For the second, use \(e>2\). For the third, use \(\sqrt{128}<12\) and \(e^8>2^8\), giving the bound
\(240e^{-8}/\sqrt k<15/16\).
Their sum is less than one.

For \(1\le s\le s_{\max}\), the global scalar bounds after (4), together with (1), instead give
$$
\mu^{[j]}(s)\le32k,\qquad
L^{[j]}(s)\le40\sqrt{258k}<680\sqrt k,\qquad
\mu^{[j]}(s)+L^{[j]}(s)<712k<B. \tag{8}
$$
Indeed \(V_s^{[j]}/s^2<256j/s^2+2(k-j)\le258k\).

The derivative identity
\((\Psi^{[j]})'=\mathcal F'-\mu^{[j]}-L^{[j]}\), interpreted one-sidedly at a breakpoint of \(\mathcal F\), follows from the scalar identities above. Equations (6)-(8) show that both one-sided derivatives of \(\Psi^{[j]}\) are positive throughout \([\bar s,s_{\max}]\). This continuous function is piecewise continuously differentiable, with finitely many breakpoints from \(\mathcal F\), and is therefore strictly increasing there. Its left derivative at \(\bar s\) is positive too, so \(\bar s\) itself cannot be a minimizer. At zero the unique active height of \(\mathcal F\) is zero; since \(L^{[j]}(0)>0\) and the mean is nonnegative, the right derivative of \(\Psi^{[j]}\) is strictly negative. Compactness gives a global minimizer, and every such minimizer lies in \((0,\bar s)\).

Fix any one of these minimizing rates, and write
\(s=s_j\), \(v=s_jB\), \(U=ks_j^2\), and \(V=V_{s_j}^{[j]}\).
The unscripted \(V\) is precisely this total radius. At an interior minimum, the one-sided derivative condition gives
$$
\min\mathcal J(s_j)\le\mu^{[j]}(s_j)+L^{[j]}(s_j)
 \le\max\mathcal J(s_j)\le2B.
$$
As the mean is nonnegative, it follows that
$$
L^{[j]}(s_j)\le2B,\qquad
V\le\frac{v^2}{400},\qquad
U\le k\bar s^2\le\frac{900}{2^{32}k}<1. \tag{9}
$$
These estimates hold for every global minimizer.

We next lower bound this radius using the canonical conditional imbalance. At root \(1\) of a full coordinate, the two nonzero displacements have imbalance \(b=\pm B/2\). Their total joint probability under the scalar root/displacement law is exactly
$$
\Pr(J_i=1,\ |V_i|=1)=\frac{2qK_s(1)^2}{P(s)}. \tag{10}
$$
Indeed, the root has probability \(K_s(1)^3/P(s)\), and the conditional probability of these two displacements is \(2q/K_s(1)\), by (3) after factoring out the common root-energy factor. The random variable \(V_i\) in (10) is the displacement defined in the statement, as in accepted \(69083720ffaaff7c\), whereas \(V\) in (9) is the summed radius.

Since \(s<1/100\), we have \(K_s(1)^2\ge e^{-8s/3}>3/4\).
The bound \(P\le56\) makes (10) at least \(3q/112\). Its contribution of \(b^2\) to \(R_i\) is therefore at least \(3v^2q/448\). The \(j\) full coordinates give \(V\ge3jv^2q/448\), so (9) implies
$$
jq\le\frac{28}{75}<\frac12. \tag{11}
$$
If \(v\le1\), then \(q\ge e^{-2/3}>1/2\), contradicting \(j\ge1\) and (11). For the strict inequality, one elementary proof is
\(\log2=2\int_0^{1/3}(1-y^2)^{-1}\,dy>2/3\).
Hence \(v>1\) at every minimizing rate.

For \(v>1\), equation (3) gives \(P<16\). In fact
\(q<e^{-2/3}<2/3\), \(e^{-4v}<1/16\), and \(2v-u\ge v\), whence
$$
P<1+(7/3)^3+28/16<16.
$$
Here \(e^{2/3}>1+2/3>3/2\) gives \(e^{-2/3}<2/3\), and \(e>2\) gives the other exponential bound. Now (10) is at least \(3q/32\); its imbalance contribution and (9) yield the sharper inequalities
$$
V\ge\frac{3jv^2q}{128},\qquad
jq\le\frac8{75}. \tag{12}
$$
Also \(V\ge U\), from the leading \(1\) in every coordinate's definition of \(R_i/s^2\).

It remains to compare surplus to radius. Expanding the root-\(1\) cube in (3), using \(e^{-4u/3}\le1\) and \(q\le1\), bounds its increment over \(e^{-4u}\) by
\(6q+12q^2+8q^3\le26q\). The other two roots contribute at most
\(28e^{-4v}\le28q\). Therefore \(P-P_{\rm bin}\le54q\).
The four-site scalar normalizer \(Z_i(s)\) is at least the binary scalar normalizer, and \(P_{\rm bin}\ge1\), so
$$
\delta_{\rm four}(s)
 \le\delta_{\rm bin}(s)+\log\frac{P(s)}{P_{\rm bin}(s)}
 \le\delta_{\rm bin}(s)+54q.
$$
Combining (2), (9), and (12) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\delta_i^{[j]}(s_j)&\le2U+54jq,\\
2U&\le2\sqrt V,\\
54jq&\le54\sqrt{8/75}\sqrt{128/3}\,
       \frac{\sqrt V}{v}
       <\frac{576}{5}\sqrt V.
\end{aligned}
$$
For the second line, use \(U<1\) and \(V\ge U\). For the last, use \(v>1\) and the two bounds in (12).
Their sum proves (C), and therefore strictly fails (A), including its additional positive term \(4s_j\). This holds for every prefix and every choice of its global minimizing rate. The rule necessarily selects \(j=0\).

To locate its active heights, the established \(v>1\) says \(s_j>1/B\). For every integer \(t\le B\), the forward increment of
\(\log(f_t/f_0)+s_jt\) is positive, since its largest logarithmic cost in this range is
\(\log((B+1)/B)<1/B<s_j\). No such \(t\) is active; every active height is at least \(B+1>T/2\), as stated. In addition, (12) gives
\(v\ge(3/2)\log(75j/8)\), so every
\(j\ge\lceil(8/75)e^{16}\rceil\) has \(v\ge24\).
Thus arbitrarily large prefixes lie in the expensive near-binary scalar regime while their active heights remain above half the cap.

Finally, compute the loss directly in the original finite-cap law. Every binary spatial vector is feasible, and its height interval has \(2B-|\mathbf x|+1\) atoms. Since \(\beta=0\), each such atom has unnormalized weight one. Thus
$$
Z_{\rm bin}
 =\sum_{\mathbf x\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k}(2B-|\mathbf x|+1)
 =2^k(2B+1-k/2)\le(2B+1)2^k.
$$
For each \(i\), consider the sector with \(x_i=2\) and all other coordinates binary. Every one of its \(2^{k-1}\) spatial vectors is feasible, since \(B\ge2k\). Its height interval has at least
\(B-k+2\ge B/2\) atoms. The original mass of that sector is consequently at least \((B/2)2^{k-1}\). These \(k\) sectors and the binary sector are pairwise disjoint subsets of the complete original support. Hence
$$
\frac{Z}{Z_{\rm bin}}
 \ge1+\frac{k(B/2)2^{k-1}}{(2B+1)2^k}
 =1+\frac{kB}{4(2B+1)}
 \ge1+\frac{k}{12},
$$
because \(2B+1\le3B\). This proves (D). For any proposed absolute finite mass-loss constant, a sufficiently large finite integer \(k\) violates it.

The sectors producing this loss have a coordinate at site \(2\); fourth-site-only deletion retains all of them. The computation therefore refutes only the rule that deletes both sites \(2\) and \(3\). It provides no upper bound on the original cubic depth moment and no disproof of that moment's desired lower bound.
statement:
The following defines the precise rule being refuted. All logarithms are natural. Let \(k\ge1\), \(T\ge1\), and the costs \(2\le B_1\le\cdots\le B_k\), \(C_{4,i}\ge2B_i-1\) be integers, and let \(\beta\ge0\) be real. On \(\lbrace0,1,2,3\rbrace\), set \(g_i=(0,1,B_i,C_{4,i})\). For \(0\le j\le k\), restrict coordinate \(i\) to
$$
D_i^{[j]}=
\begin{cases}
\lbrace0,1,2,3\rbrace,&i\le j,\\
\lbrace0,1\rbrace,&i>j.
\end{cases}
$$
The restricted potential \(g_i^{[j]}\) is the original \(g_i\) on that interval. In the common ambient space \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\), define the complete retained epigraph law by
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma^{[j]}(\mathbf x)&=\sum_i g_i^{[j]}(x_i),\\
A_T^{[j]}&=\left\lbrace(\mathbf x,t):
  \mathbf x\in\prod_iD_i^{[j]},\ t\in\mathbb Z,\
  \Gamma^{[j]}(\mathbf x)\le t\le T\right\rbrace,\\
Z^{[j]}&=\sum_{(\mathbf x,t)\in A_T^{[j]}}e^{-\beta t},
\qquad
p^{[j]}_{(\mathbf x,t)}=\frac{e^{-\beta t}}{Z^{[j]}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Write \(Z=Z^{[k]}\) and \(Z_{\rm bin}=Z^{[0]}\). Thus restriction deletes atoms and then renormalizes; every retained atom keeps its original unnormalized weight.

Here are the scalar quantities defining the rule. They are the scalar objects of accepted \(69083720ffaaff7c\), with the displacement domain restricted to \(D_i^{[j]}\). To give their full meaning, fix a prefix \(j\), and temporarily suppress that superscript. For \(\lambda\in D_i^{[j]}\), put
$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{i,\lambda}&=\left\lbrace h\in\mathbb Z:
   \lambda+h,\lambda-h\in D_i^{[j]}\right\rbrace,\\
e_{i,\lambda}(h)&=
 \tfrac12\bigl(g_i(\lambda+h)+g_i(\lambda-h)\bigr)-g_i(\lambda),\\
b_{i,\lambda}(h)&=
 \tfrac12\bigl(g_i(\lambda+h)-g_i(\lambda-h)\bigr),\\
K_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\sum_{h\in I_{i,\lambda}}
 \exp\left(-\tfrac{2s}{3}\bigl(g_i(\lambda+h)+g_i(\lambda-h)\bigr)\right),\\
H_{s,i}(\lambda)&=\sum_{h\in I_{i,\lambda}}
 \exp\left(-\tfrac{4s}{3}e_{i,\lambda}(h)\right),\\
P_i(s)&=\sum_{\lambda\in D_i^{[j]}}K_{s,i}(\lambda)^3,\qquad
Z_i(s)=\sum_{\lambda\in D_i^{[j]}}e^{-s g_i(\lambda)},\\
\delta_i(s)&=\log\frac{8P_i(s)}{Z_i(s)^4},
\qquad
Q_{s,i}(\lambda)=\frac{K_{s,i}(\lambda)^3}{P_i(s)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Let \(J_i\) have law \(Q_{s,i}\); conditionally on \(J_i=\lambda\), let the displacement \(V_i\) have probabilities \(e^{-(4s/3)e_{i,\lambda}(h)}/H_{s,i}(\lambda)\). Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i(s)&=\mathbb E\bigl[g_i(J_i)+e_{i,J_i}(V_i)\bigr],\\
R_i(s)&=s^2\left(1+\mathbb E\left[
 g_i(J_i)^2+e_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2+b_{i,J_i}(V_i)^2\right]\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
The conditional imbalance second moment, if named, is
\(\sigma^b_{s,i}(\lambda)=\mathbb E[b_{i,\lambda}(V_i)^2\mid J_i=\lambda]\), exactly as in \(69083720ffaaff7c\). These auxiliary counting laws are defined directly; no conditional product property of \(p^{[j]}\) is assumed. Restore the superscript \([j]\) on these scalar quantities, and put
$$
\mu^{[j]}(s)=\sum_i\mu_i^{[j]}(s),\qquad
V_s^{[j]}=\sum_iR_i^{[j]}(s),\qquad
L^{[j]}(s)=\frac{40\sqrt{V_s^{[j]}}}{s}\quad(s>0).
$$
At \(s=0\), define \(L^{[j]}\) by the continuous finite-expectation extension of this formula. In particular it is finite and positive. With \(f_t=\sum_{h=t}^T e^{-\beta h}\), define, for every mask, the same functions
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(s)&=\max_{\substack{0\le t\le T\\t\in\mathbb Z}}
 \left(\log(f_t/f_0)+st\right),\\
\mathcal J(s)&=\mathop{\rm argmax}_{\substack{0\le t\le T\\t\in\mathbb Z}}
 \left(\log(f_t/f_0)+st\right),\\
\Psi^{[j]}(s)&=\mathcal F(s)+\frac14\sum_i\log P_i^{[j]}(s)
 -\int_0^sL^{[j]}(y)\,dy,\qquad
0\le s\le s_{\max}:=12\log2.
\end{aligned}
$$
For every \(1\le j\le k\), choose an arbitrary global minimizer \(s_j\) of \(\Psi^{[j]}\) on this compact interval. Call \(j\) successful if \(0<s_j<s_{\max}\) and
$$
\sum_i\delta_i^{[j]}(s_j)
 \ge256\sqrt{V_{s_j}^{[j]}}+4s_j. \tag{A}
$$
Retain the largest successful prefix, and retain \(j=0\) if none is successful. Condition (A) is the surplus condition paying the exponent in the product certificate (20) of accepted \(69083720ffaaff7c\). In particular each mask in this rule is tested at its own adaptive minimizing rate.

For every integer \(k\ge1\), consider the finite legal family
$$
B=2^{16}k^2,\qquad B_i=B,\qquad C_{4,i}=2B-1,
\qquad T=2B,\qquad\beta=0. \tag{B}
$$
For this family, every global minimizer for every \(1\le j\le k\) lies in \((0,s_{\max})\), every active height at that minimizer is at least \(B+1>T/2\), and
$$
\sum_i\delta_i^{[j]}(s_j)
 <\frac{586}{5}\sqrt{V_{s_j}^{[j]}}
 <256\sqrt{V_{s_j}^{[j]}}. \tag{C}
$$
Thus no nonempty prefix is successful, independently of any choice among minimizing rates. The rule selects the all-binary law, but
$$
\frac{Z}{Z_{\rm bin}}\ge1+\frac{k}{12}. \tag{D}
$$
Consequently no absolute finite constant bounds the original-mass loss of this rule over the displayed legal data.

This statement concerns deletion of both sites \(2\) and \(3\) outside the selected prefix. It makes no assertion of a failure for fourth-site-only deletion and no assertion that the original cubic depth moment violates any lower bound. The symbols \(n,d,C,W,c_0\) retain their locked meanings.
